name: Tracking Synergies After a Merger
title: Tracking Synergies After a Merger
answer: Tracking synergies after a merger is the work of measuring whether the combined company delivers the cost savings and revenue gains that justified the deal. In private equity, this covers portfolio companies bought on a synergy thesis, where the fund needs evidence that the plan is being met. The scope runs from the day the deal closes through the integration period, and it touches finance, operations and the deal team. It is distinct from deal sourcing, which looks at targets before purchase, and from standard post-close reporting, which tracks overall performance rather than the specific gains attributed to combining two businesses.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Tracking synergies after a merger is the work of measuring whether the combined company delivers the cost savings and revenue gains that justified the deal. In private equity, this covers portfolio companies bought on a synergy thesis, where the fund needs evidence that the plan is being met. The scope runs from the day the deal closes through the integration period, and it touches finance, operations and the deal team. It is distinct from deal sourcing, which looks at targets before purchase, and from standard post-close reporting, which tracks overall performance rather than the specific gains attributed to combining two businesses.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the combined company's financial systems, which rarely talk to each other at close, so the first task is often a common chart of accounts and a single reporting calendar. Deal teams use spreadsheets and business intelligence tools for the tracking model, and increasingly pull data from ERP and HR systems rather than waiting for monthly packs. Where the fund holds several portfolio companies, a shared reporting platform is common so that synergy claims can be compared across deals. Public filings and the site's merger and acquisition filings can supply benchmarks for what similar deals claimed and disclosed.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual method is to build a baseline for each synergy, stating what the cost or revenue line would have been without the deal, then measure actuals against it at fixed intervals. Cost synergies such as headcount reduction or procurement savings are tracked against budget lines, while revenue synergies such as cross-selling are harder and often tracked through pipeline and customer data. Each item gets an owner, a value and a date, and the tracker is reviewed in an integration committee. Variance is investigated rather than simply reported, because a missed synergy may be a timing issue or a genuine shortfall.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Synergy tracking sits inside the fund's obligations to its own investors, and overstated numbers can become a problem at the next fundraise or in a dispute with a seller over earn-outs. The finance team owns the numbers, and auditors or the fund's own controls may test how the baseline was set. Where the deal involved public companies, disclosure rules govern what can be said about expected synergies, and the site's compliance and regulation pages cover the wider rule set. Records of how each figure was calculated should be kept, because the value of the tracker depends on being able to defend it later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous tracking rather than quarterly packs, with data pulled directly from source systems and dashboards that update as transactions post. Machine learning is being applied to separate genuine synergy from market movement, which is the hardest part of the baseline problem. Funds are also under pressure to show that synergy claims made at deal time were actually delivered, which pushes toward standard definitions across a portfolio. Over time the tracker is likely to merge with ordinary performance reporting, so that the question of what the deal added is answered by the same system that answers how the company is doing.
